b: Most anglers have seen their share of unusual catches, but this one might be tough to top.

Biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) recently pulled a remarkably colored burbot from Oswego Harbor, New York. Instead of the usual brown and olive tones, this fish was sporting a bright yellow-orange color that looked more like a Halloween pumpkin than a bottom-dwelling Great Lakes fish.

The unusual coloration is known as xanthochromism, a rare pigmentation condition generally associated with genetic changes that produce yellow or orange coloring. And while oddly colored fish occasionally turn up in anglers’ catches, finding one like this in the wild is a pretty special occurrence.
A Rare Fish in an Unusual Place
A biologist holds up a rare xanthochromismistic burbot caught during survey. Courtesy US Fish and Wildlife Service
The burbot (Lota lota) was collected during a routine aquatic invasive species survey conducted by USFWS biologists.

Burbot are native to the Great Lakes and are the only freshwater members of the cod family. Sometimes called eelpout or lawyer, they’re coldwater fish that typically inhabit deeper, cooler water, often holding near rocky bottoms.
They’re also not particularly common in Lake Ontario these days. Burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, making any encounter noteworthy.
According to fisheries biologists, this is the first documented burbot captured during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although anglers have reported catching a few over the years.
Finding one in the harbor was interesting enough. Finding one with a bright golden-orange complexion made it that much more unusual.
What Makes a Fish Turn Orange?
Lateral view of a common snook, Centropomus undecimalis, with xanthochromism caught in the southern Gulf near Mexico.

The condition responsible for the burbot’s unusual appearance is called xanthochromism, sometimes referred to as xanthism. It’s an uncommon pigmentation variation that results in yellow or orange coloration. And it’s not limited to burbot.

Anglers have occasionally encountered unusually colored bass, crappie, gar, and other freshwater species. Saltwater examples include grouper, triggerfish, and tripletail. Even sharks and snook have turned up with unusual yellow or orange colorations. Similar pigmentation variations occur in other wildlife, including birds and frogs.

While the exact genetic mechanisms can vary between species, xanthochromism is generally associated with changes in pigment production that cause an animal to display more yellow or orange coloration than normal.

For fish, that can be a serious disadvantage. Most fish rely on natural camouflage to avoid becoming somebody else’s lunch. A smallmouth bass usually blends in with rocky bottoms thanks to its bronze and brown coloring. A burbot’s typical dark, mottled appearance similarly helps it disappear against the lake bottom.

But a bright orange fish doesn’t have quite the same advantage. Scientists believe unusually colored fish may be especially vulnerable to predators when they’re young and small. Those surviving into adulthood are likely the lucky exceptions.
It’s also why brightly colored fish are popular in the aquarium trade, where breeders sometimes selectively produce unusual color variations without the threat of hungry predators.
Not Every Oddly Colored Fish Is an Albino
Have you ever caught an orange bass? The coloration on this bass is very uncommon. Courtesy of Wildwood Resort and Marina on Facebook
Xanthochromism is just one of several color variations anglers might encounter.

Melanism, for example, produces unusually dark fish due to increased melanin, the pigment responsible for dark coloration. Some smallmouth bass can appear almost black, depending on their genetics and environmental conditions.

Albinism is different. Albino fish lack the ability to produce melanin, and may have pale bodies and reddish or pinkish eyes. Leucistic fish also appear unusually pale but generally retain normal eye pigmentation.
Then there’s hypomelanism, which results in reduced dark pigmentation and can make fish look washed out or unusually light.
These conditions can have different causes, ranging from genetics to environmental influences and health issues.
The Fish Wasn’t in Great Shape

As impressive as the burbot’s appearance was, experts noticed something concerning when they examined the fish. United States Geological Survey fisheries biologists familiar with the species observed that it was emaciated and appeared to be in poor health.
Given the fish’s condition, along with the ongoing questions surrounding the low numbers of burbot in Lake Ontario, researchers decided to take a closer look.

The fish was sent to Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis. That examination could help scientists better understand what might be affecting burbot in the Lake Ontario basin. While one fish certainly can’t tell the whole story, individual specimens can provide valuable information about health concerns and potential factors limiting a population.
